reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A typically benign neuronal tumour (CNS WHO grade 2) of young and middle-aged adults, arising within the lateral ventricles
Characteristically attached near the septum pellucidum or foramen of Monro, where it obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow
Usually presents with headache and other features of raised intracranial pressure from obstructive hydrocephalus
Histology resembles oligodendroglioma with uniform round cells, but neuronal differentiation is confirmed by strong synaptophysin positivity
Retained ATRX and absence of IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion help distinguish it from oligodendroglioma
Extraventricular neurocytomas with similar morphology can occur in the brain parenchyma
Gross total resection is often curative; atypical variants with higher proliferation may recur
reference.pathophysiology: Central neurocytoma is a neuronal tumour believed to arise from bipotential progenitor cells or neuronal precursors near the septum pellucidum and the walls of the lateral ventricles. It grows as a well-circumscribed intraventricular mass composed of uniform round cells with clear cytoplasm and finely speckled chromatin, set in a fibrillary neuropil-like background, frequently with calcification and microcystic change. Despite a superficial resemblance to oligodendroglioma on light microscopy, it shows neuronal differentiation demonstrated by synaptophysin expression and lacks the molecular signatures of diffuse glioma. Symptoms result largely from mechanical obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid at the foramen of Monro.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the intraventricular mass and hydrocephalus
Assessment of relationship to the septum pellucidum and foramen of Monro
Histopathology showing uniform round cells in a neuropil background
Synaptophysin immunohistochemistry to confirm neuronal differentiation
IDH, 1p/19q and ATRX testing to exclude oligodendroglioma
Ki-67/MIB-1 proliferation index to identify atypical, higher-risk tumours
redFlags: Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with rapidly rising intracranial pressure
High proliferation index or atypical features indicating recurrence risk
Sudden deterioration in consciousness from cerebrospinal fluid obstruction
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable, with gross total resection frequently curative and long-term survival common. Atypical central neurocytomas with an elevated proliferation index carry a higher risk of recurrence, and adjuvant radiotherapy may be considered for incompletely resected or recurrent disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as oligodendroglioma and applying inappropriate glioma management
Not performing synaptophysin staining to establish neuronal differentiation
Overlooking an elevated proliferation index that flags an atypical, recurrence-prone tumour
Delaying relief of obstructive hydrocephalus in a symptomatic patient
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: For acute obstructive hydrocephalus, urgently relieve CSF obstruction via external ventricular drain, endoscopic third ventriculostomy, or shunt, either before or at the time of definitive surgery.
Maximal safe surgical resection is the primary and usually definitive treatment for localized, resectable tumors, with gross total resection frequently curative.
Choice of transcortical versus transcallosal surgical approach is made by the neurosurgical team based on ventricular anatomy and tumor extent.
Consider adjuvant radiotherapy for incompletely resected, recurrent, or atypical tumors with an elevated proliferation index or atypical histology.
Stereotactic radiosurgery is a reasonable option for small residual or recurrent disease, especially where repeat open resection carries high risk.
Systemic drug therapy has no established role in central neurocytoma; management relies on local therapy (surgery and radiotherapy when indicated) rather than systemic anticancer regimens.

Typical sequence is maximal safe resection, then surveillance imaging if resection is complete and histology is typical, with adjuvant radiotherapy reserved for incomplete resection, atypical histology, or recurrence.
At recurrence, individualize repeat resection and/or radiotherapy through the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team.
Obtain serial contrast-enhanced brain MRI to monitor for recurrence or progression, with surveillance intervals individualized to extent of resection and histologic risk.
Monitor clinically for symptoms of raised intracranial pressure or new hydrocephalus, prompting urgent imaging if present.
Confirm diagnosis histopathologically with synaptophysin staining and assess proliferation index (Ki-67/MIB-1) to stratify standard versus atypical, higher-recurrence-risk disease.
Refer newly identified intraventricular masses suspicious for central neurocytoma to an experienced neurosurgical team and to a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team once histology is confirmed.
Refer urgently to neurosurgery for acute or rapidly progressive obstructive hydrocephalus or deteriorating consciousness.

Pursue neuropathology review including IDH, 1p/19q, and ATRX status when the differential with oligodendroglioma or another glial tumor is unresolved, since management differs substantially between these entities.
